articles.title: Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
articles.summary: The jump in Nvidia shares has also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq up 6.5%.
articles.body:
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.

Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.

Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday , with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.

Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.

Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.

While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.

A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.

Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".

"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.

"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.

"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.

"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.

"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."

Politicians are also demanding greater scrutiny.

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."

She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."

articles.title: A 15-year-old waitress earning £7 an hour at a Scottish hotel was screamed and sworn at for dropping a plate of apple crumble; a tribunal has now ordered her bosses to pay her more than £13,000
articles.summary: A teenage waitress who was shouted at and sworn at by senior staff after accidentally dropping a plate of apple crumble has been awarded £13,048 by an
articles.body: A teenage waitress who was shouted at and sworn at by senior staff after accidentally dropping a plate of apple crumble has been awarded £13,048 by an employment tribunal in Scotland. Daniesha Charles was just 15 when she worked at the Royal Thurso Hotel in the Scottish Highlands, earning £7 an hour. The incident was among several episodes of mistreatment she experienced during her short time at the hotel. The tribunal found that the treatment amounted to discrimination and harassment linked to her age, sex and race, as well as disability in some instances.What happened to the 15-year-old waitress over the dropped apple crumbleAccording to the employment tribunal judgment in Miss D Charles v Thurso Hotel Limited, Daniesha Charles worked at the hotel between 1 May and 26 June 2024. She was employed on a casual, zero-hours basis while attending a full-time college course three days a week. Her agreed hourly pay was £7, and she was not guaranteed a fixed number of shifts.The incident involving the apple crumble took place on 26 June 2024, when she was serving dessert to the final table of a large coach party. As she walked through the kitchen's swinging doors, one of the doors swung back and knocked the plate from her hand.Charles returned to the kitchen to explain what had happened and intended to ask the chef for another portion to serve the guest. However, the chef interrupted her, reportedly responding with the words ‘ofcourse you did.’The situation quickly escalated when the chef and hotel general manager, Andy Woodcock, began shouting and swearing at her. According to the tribunal's findings, both men repeatedly used offensive language during the confrontation.The teenager eventually broke down in tears and shouted back, asking them to stop treating her that way. Instead, both men told her to get out. As she left the kitchen, someone also began pulling her apron from behind.The findings were recorded in the official employment tribunal judgment, which described the incident as an episode of abusive treatment that violated her dignity.Earlier incidents had already made her workplace difficultThe apple crumble incident was not the first time Charles had experienced hostile behaviour from the kitchen staff. The tribunal examined two other episodes that took place during her employment.During her first week, she struggled to hold an extremely hot plate because she did not have adequate hand protection. Rather than helping her, the chef shouted and swore at her. She later described feeling intimidated, frightened and nervous following the incident.Another confrontation occurred in May 2024, when Charles misspelt the word porridge on a breakfast order slip. Her severe dyslexia made spelling and writing difficult, a condition she had already disclosed to Woodcock during her job interview.When the chef noticed the spelling mistake, he reportedly shouted that it was not how she spelt porridge, using an expletive in front of other employees. The incident left her feeling humiliated and embarrassed.According to the tribunal, the chef had displayed contempt towards her from the beginning of her employment, repeatedly referring to her as that and it rather than addressing her by name. The official judgment also noted that she was the youngest member of staff and one of only a small number of non-white employees at the hotel.Why did the employment tribunal find discriminationCharles was a Black British Caribbean teenager with severe dyslexia. The tribunal found that the treatment she experienced was not simply a case of managers losing their temper during busy working hours.It heard evidence that the chef and Woodcock had shouted and sworn at younger employees, female workers and members of staff from non-white backgrounds. However, they had not behaved similarly towards older white British male employees.The tribunal considered this difference important when examining her discrimination complaints. It found that the treatment was connected to her protected characteristics, including age, sex and race. The porridge incident also involved disability discrimination because her spelling difficulty was linked to her severe dyslexia.The tribunal decided that the behaviour amounted to harassment because it violated her dignity and created an intimidating, hostile, degrading and humiliating working environment.The case also involved the way her employment ended. After Charles left the hotel, her mother, Stacey Charles, contacted the management to complain about the treatment.In an email dated 30 June 2024, Woodcock said that had the hotel known about her anxieties and depression before employing her, it would not have placed her in that working environment. He also stated that ending her employment was the only option at that point.The tribunal interpreted the email as evidence that the hotel had ended her contract because of a disability it believed she had. It ruled that this amounted to direct discrimination based on perceived disability.How the £13,048 compensation was calculatedThe employment tribunal hearing took place remotely in Edinburgh on 19 and 20 August 2026 before Employment Judge JG d'Inverno. Charles attended without legal representation and was supported by her mother. The hotel did not send anyone to represent it at the final hearing, although it had previously submitted a response denying the discrimination allegations while admitting that the chef and general manager had shouted and sworn.The tribunal accepted Charles's evidence and found that the hotel had failed to provide her with written particulars of employment, as required under employment law.It awarded her a total of £13,048, divided into 3 parts. The largest amount, £11,500, was awarded for the emotional distress caused by the discriminatory treatment. A further £1,032 covered 6 weeks of lost earnings following the termination of her contract. The remaining £516 was compensation for the hotel's failure to provide written employment terms.The tribunal noted that Charles had initially sought £58,700 for injury to feelings. However, it considered the lower amount appropriate after assessing the three main incidents and their impact on her.Following the tribunal decision, the Royal Thurso Hotel issued a public statement addressing the findings. According to a report by the Press and Journal, the business stressed that it was now operating under a completely new management and kitchen team.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A £750,000 payment to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, later repaid, branded a possible ‘bribe’ over Turkish woman's passport; Sarah Ferguson and Princess Beatrice named in High Court row
articles.summary: A £750,000 payment to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, made in 2019 and later repaid, has resurfaced in a London courtroom, raising fresh questions about the
articles.body: A £750,000 payment to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, made in 2019 and later repaid, has resurfaced in a London courtroom, raising fresh questions about the circumstances surrounding the transaction. What was initially described as a gift has now become the subject of a heated legal dispute, with lawyers suggesting that the money could have been a possible “bribe” linked to helping a Turkish woman secure her passport or UK residency.The controversy has emerged during a High Court battle involving Turkish businesswoman Nebahat Isbilen and her former financial adviser, Selman Turk. Isbilen has accused Turk of misappropriating millions of pounds and misleading her about several financial transactions, including the substantial payment made to the former Duke of York.The case has taken another turn as payments allegedly involving Sarah Ferguson and Princess Beatrice have also come under scrutiny. While Andrew is not accused of any wrongdoing, his expected appearance as a witness could bring further attention to the circumstances surrounding the £750,000 transaction.How a Turkish businesswoman's millions became part of a royal money trailAt the centre of the legal battle is Nebahat Isbilen, an 81-year-old member of Turkey's wealthy Evyap family, which owns a major soap and cosmetics business. She claims that the man she trusted with her finances, businessman Selman Turk, misappropriated tens of millions of pounds and failed to explain where the money went.As reported by The Mirror, the dispute dates back to 2017, when Isbilen was facing difficulties in Turkey. Her husband, a former member of the Turkish parliament, had been imprisoned since 2015 on terrorism charges that she believes were politically motivated.According to her barrister, Simon Colton KC, Isbilen met Turk in January 2017 and eventually handed him control of most of her financial assets. He allegedly convinced her that her wealth was at risk and that he could move it somewhere safe.However, her legal team claims that what followed was a systematic abuse of trust. Colton told the court that Turk transferred money to companies he owned or controlled, allegedly using the funds for his own benefit. He also claimed that Isbilen was persuaded to sign financial documents that did not reflect what she had been told about her money.Why was £750,000 paid to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor?Among the transactions now being examined is the £750,000 payment made to Andrew in 2019. According to Isbilen's legal team, she approved the transaction but was allegedly misled by Turk about its purpose.Her lawyers claim that Turk presented the payment as a gift connected to Andrew's possible assistance with her passport or UK residency. They argue that the explanation was false and that the transaction was another example of the businessman's alleged dishonesty.Documents obtained during the proceedings reportedly revealed that around £2 million had been transferred to a company called Alphabet Capital, with some of the money subsequently reaching Andrew.The payment has become a particularly sensitive part of the case because of the questions surrounding why such a substantial sum was transferred and what was expected in return.Andrew, however, is not accused of wrongdoing in the proceedings.Sarah Ferguson and Princess Beatrice also surface in the caseThe financial trail does not end with Andrew. Sarah Ferguson and Princess Beatrice have also been mentioned during the proceedings over separate payments allegedly arranged by Turk.The court heard that Sarah received a payment of £15,000, reportedly intended for her 60th birthday celebrations in 2019. A separate amount, described as a wedding gift for Princess Beatrice, was also mentioned, although the exact figure was not disclosed.Another transaction involved approximately 275,000 US dollars (around £210,000) being transferred by a bank to Alphabet Capital on Turk's instructions. According to Isbilen's legal team, most of that money was subsequently paid to Sarah.The High Court had previously been told in 2023 that Isbilen had reached a settlement with Andrew and Sarah.Selman Turk denies wrongdoing, claims businesswoman knew about the paymentTurk has strongly disputed the allegations and is defending the claim. His barrister, Joshua Hitchens, challenged Isbilen's account, describing her case as a “mess” that should be dismissed.The defence argues that Isbilen knew the purpose of the £750,000 payment and understood that it was intended to secure Andrew's assistance, either with her passport or her UK residency.Hitchens told the court that Isbilen had authorised the transactions herself. He also referred to a private dinner in December 2019, attended by Isbilen, Turk, Andrew and Sarah, during which she allegedly discussed her husband's situation with the former prince.According to the defence, the payment was a gift made in the hope that Andrew would take steps to help her husband. Hitchens argued that Isbilen could not have believed the money was a disguised fee for passport or visa assistance when she had personally met the duke and discussed her husband's case with him.Turk's lawyers also maintain that Isbilen understood and directed the management of her own financial affairs.Andrew summoned to appear before the High CourtThe case could take another significant turn on December 14, when Andrew is due to give evidence. Earlier this year, a judge allowed Turk to issue a witness summons compelling the former prince to appear at the trial.His testimony could bring further clarity to the circumstances surrounding the £750,000 payment and the discussions that allegedly took place between him and Isbilen.The trial, being heard by Mr Justice Adam Johnson, is expected to conclude in March, with a written judgment to follow.You use AI every day. articles.title: Concerns over sewage discharge on to dry riverbed in Peterchurch
articles.summary: Campaigners call for restrictions on sewage treatment plant discharging effluent during drought
articles.body:
A group of residents have said pools of treated sewage are forming on a dry riverbed that runs through their village during drought conditions.

They are calling for the Environment Agency to stop the sewage treatment plant in Peterchurch, Herefordshire, discharging into the River Dore during periods of no flow.

At the moment, Welsh Water legally discharges directly into the river, but campaigners said its permit assumed the effluent would be diluted by the river flow.

The company said the plant was operating in accordance with the permit, but it was liaising with residents over their concerns.

Locals have formed a Citizen's Science Project for the Dore catchment and say lab tests have shown the waste contains "high levels of nitrate and phosphorus" as well as harmful bacteria including "worrying amounts of E. coli".

Alice Elliott from the group said they had seen periods of drought affecting the river level for several years:

"Where the river stops flowing it goes completely dry, absolutely no flow.

"The sewage treatment works is continually discharging onto a dry riverbed and it's created a large pool of treated but undiluted effluent."

The group said it had samples from the site tested in a laboratory and were seeing "high levels of nitrate and phosphorus".

"Treated effluent isn't clean sanitised water." said Elliott.

"We've noticed that it contains worrying amounts of E. coli and other bacteria that are harmful to health... Normally it would get diluted down and that's what the permit allows".

It is thought the area is surrounded by a permeable gravel bed and residents are concerned the "extensive pool" is being allowed to "permeate through the ground and through the soil around it."

The dry bed also becomes a lure for children playing during drought conditions.

"It was like a sunken road, it was an exciting environment and the children were skipping along, unaware that a few metres away is a big pool of treated sewage."

The group has demanded answers from both Welsh Water and the Environment Agency.

"What we've asked is how do they go about assessing and issuing their permits for Welsh Water? What are they doing in terms of assessing the environmental impact when they know there is a period of no flow. What action... what plans are they putting in place to combat that?" said Elliott.

The River Dore flows into the Monnow, which then joins the River Wye at Monmouth - a river that has had it's fair share of publicity over alleged contamination, leading to it becoming the first river in the UK to get its own special protection charter.

An Environment Agency spokesperson said: "Protecting and improving water quality is a priority for the Environment Agency, and we understand the concerns raised by local residents about conditions in the River Dore during prolonged dry weather.

"Peterchurch sewage treatment works' discharge is permitted and currently understood to be compliant. We continue to monitor conditions in the River Dore."

"Peterchurch waste water treatment works is operating as it should and within the permit conditions issued by our regulator.

"The treated effluent is routinely sampled and tested and we are liaising with the Dore Citizen Science group and the Environment Agency on this matter."

articles.title: US army veteran mauled to death by pack of dogs in Georgia, daughter demands justice
articles.summary: A 36-year-old US Army veteran and mother of three was mauled to death in an attack by a pack of dogs in Georgia, leaving her pregnant daughter devastated
articles.body: A 36-year-old US Army veteran and mother of three was mauled to death in an attack by a pack of dogs in Georgia, leaving her pregnant daughter devastated and demanding justice. Allison Lynn Anderson was unaware that she was about to become a grandmother for the first time when she died in the attack, the New York Post reported.Anderson was found with fatal injuries on November 16 in a field in Cartersville, Georgia, after police responded to reports of an unresponsive woman. Preliminary autopsy findings indicated that she had suffered fatal injuries, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation (GBI) said in a November 19 statement.The attack reportedly took place in the yard of an abandoned property. Authorities have not disclosed the exact number of dogs involved or the circumstances that led to the incident. Several dogs suspected of being involved have been taken into the custody of Bartow County Animal Control.Pregnant daughter says mother would have been excited about becoming a grandmotherAnderson's 20-year-old daughter, Miley Garner, who is expecting her first child with fiancé Jesse Jarrett, said her mother did not know she was pregnant."If my mom knew that I was carrying her first grandchild, she would be over the moon and full of excitement," Garner told WAFB, according to NYP.Garner also expressed anger over the incident, questioning why the dogs' owners had failed to keep them under control."I am so disgusted and absolutely heartbroken that the owners of these dogs did not have control over them," she said, describing what her mother went through as torture.Despite her grief, Garner said she believed her mother would have forgiven those responsible for what happened.Family remembers veteran as someone who never turned away from people in needAnderson, who joined the US Army in 2007, was remembered by her family as an outgoing person with a larger-than-life personality.In her obituary, the family described her as someone who never met a stranger and was always willing to help anyone in need, whether she knew them or not.She loved spending time outdoors, particularly near the water, and enjoyed swimming and fishing. She also had a passion for music and singing.Neighbours were left shocked by her death. Betty Mathison, who had spoken to Anderson about a week before the incident, remembered her as a kind and friendly person."She was a real sweet girl — she was so sweet," Mathison told Atlanta News First.Investigators are examining surveillance footage from the surrounding area as part of the ongoing investigation. articles.title: A Manitoba couple bought their dream riverside home in 2015, but a neighbour's roaming rescue dogs sparked years of conflict; a judge has now awarded the couple C$10,100 and their neighbour C$1,000
articles.summary: A Manitoba couple wins C$10,100 in damages following a protracted conflict over a neighbour's roaming rescue dogs, exposing tensions over property rights and animal control.
articles.body: A Manitoba couple who bought a riverside property to enjoy privacy and the surrounding woodland have been awarded C$10,100 in damages after a years-long dispute with a neighbour whose rescue dogs repeatedly entered their land. The neighbour, who had filed a lawsuit against the couple, was separately awarded C$1,000 over an incident involving broken dock boards thrown into her dog kennel, CBC News reported.The ruling was delivered by Manitoba Court of King's Bench Justice Sheldon Lanchbery on Monday last week. The judge found that both sides had trespassed on each other's property, but concluded that the neighbour's continued failure to control her dogs warranted a substantially higher damages award.The dispute began after the couple purchased their property along the Winnipeg River in the rural municipality of Alexander in 2015, according to CBS News. Their land included a wooded section with walking trails, which they valued for its seclusion.Around 2017, a woman bought the neighbouring property and began operating a dog rescue business. Despite having limited experience handling rescue animals, she allowed the dogs to move freely around her land, including areas without fencing.Justice Lanchbery described the animals as "feral" and noted that their aggressive behaviour continued even after they had been rescued. The neighbour also kept more dogs than permitted under municipal bylaws. Although the exact number was disputed, she had at least seven before the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the judgment.Dog attacks and failed attempts to resolve the disputeThe couple told the court that the presence of the animals made it difficult for them to use their own woodland. They said they avoided walking through parts of their property because they feared encountering the dogs.The male homeowner also testified that one of the animals bit his shin. He sustained a hand contusion after punching the dog, the judgment recorded.The neighbour maintained that the animals should be allowed to roam freely. They were not consistently confined to a kennel or restrained when outside it, and sometimes entered the couple's land, where they left faeces.Attempts to settle the disagreement did not produce an agreement. Justice Lanchbery described the discussions between the neighbours as "a lot of talking, but not a lot of listening".The conflict eventually involved security cameras, photographs, property surveys and disputes over the boundary separating the two homes. The neighbour placed large rocks near what she believed was the property line, but a subsequent survey commissioned by the couple indicated that her understanding of the boundary was incorrect.She later asked the couple to contribute towards the cost of a fence that would prevent her dogs from entering their land. They declined, arguing that keeping the animals under control was her responsibility.The judge observed that installing a fence between the properties could have prevented much of the conflict. Referring to American poet Robert Frost's famous poem "Mending Wall", he noted that "Building a fence between their properties could have solved their problem."Why the judge awarded damages to both neighboursThe disagreement extended beyond the dogs when the woman acquired a large dock for use on the Winnipeg River. Instead of placing it entirely on her own land, she positioned it on the couple's property. She also parked vehicles there, according to the judgment.The couple responded by putting up no-trespassing signs. Tensions escalated further when the male homeowner threw broken wooden boards from the dock into the neighbour's dog kennel.The woman subsequently filed a lawsuit against the couple, alleging trespassing. One of her dogs had suffered an eye injury, but the judge found that the available evidence did not establish that the animal had been hurt by the boards.The man acknowledged throwing the wood into the kennel but disputed that the dog was inside at the time. The court found no evidence establishing the animal's presence there during the incident.Justice Lanchbery ultimately ruled that both parties had trespassed. The couple were responsible for throwing the broken boards into the kennel, while the neighbour had trespassed by allowing her dogs to roam onto their property.However, the judge distinguished between the nature and frequency of their conduct. The neighbour's failure to control the animals had continued over an extended period, whereas the couple's actions involving the boards amounted to a single incident.He awarded the couple C$10,000 in general and aggravated damages over the ongoing problems caused by the dogs. An additional C$100 was granted because the neighbour had placed her dock and parked vehicles on their land, which the judge described as "an inconvenience at best".The neighbour received C$1,000 in damages over the broken-board incident. The judge called the man's actions "especially egregious", noting his previous military experience, which included training others in hand-to-hand combat.The couple's lawyer had argued that the man had shown restraint by not physically harming the dogs. However, the judge rejected that reasoning, finding that throwing the boards into the kennel was an intentional act of intimidation.Neither party was awarded legal costs. Justice Lanchbery said their conduct throughout the proceedings did not justify ordering one side to pay the other's expenses.Reflecting on the dispute, the judge wrote that by the end of the testimony, both sides were "painfully aware this was not their finest hour".You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump orders Army not to detonate explosives in Iowa without court approval
articles.summary: The US Army had said it planned to detonate the explosives on Wednesday despite a court-ordered pausea as public outcry intensified.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump said he has ordered the US army not to move ahead with plans to detonate five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa on Wednesday until a court rules on the issue.

The administration previously had planned to go forward with the plans despite legal challenges and public outcry over the potential health risks to nearby communities.

A court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation.

"I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward," Trump said, referencing the court that halted the detonation.

He added in his post on Truth Social that the US had "an opportunity to do a highly controlled detonation of these dangerous and rapidly corroding materials" because of optimal weather.

Even after the court pause ordered on Thursday, the justice department told the court that the army intends to move forward with its plan, because of an "immediate risk" that those materials could "spontaneously explode".

Environmental groups have accused the government of skirting the judicial process.

Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) says no level of lead exposure is considered safe. Lead exposure through inhalation or ingestion can pose serious health risks to humans and animals, particularly children.

The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. In its court filing on Saturday, the justice department said the army would carry out the detonation on Tuesday.

Later, in a social media post on Sunday evening, the army announced that the detonation had been rescheduled for Wednesday to allow for "optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced".

"The health and safety of all Americans has and always will be our first priority," it said.

Middletown's Mayor Rodney Johnson weighed in on Monday saying the detonation "must take place".

"It doesn't matter who dropped the ball on the removal of these expired munitions, the ball is now in November 2026 Court," Johnson said in a statement. "The buzzer is ticking and if we don't take this opportunity to Safely dispose of the problem, then actual lives may be at stake !!!"

He added that "every possible precaution" had been put into place to ensure people's safety.

The government has argued that, because this is an event that requires immediate action, the army can move forward without a permit for detonation.

The justice department's court filing describes this as an "emergency situation" in part because of the incoming cold weather.

"As the outside temperatures drop the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures," the filing said.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing stated.

It said that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion.

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club filed the legal case on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause. The advocacy groups accuse the government of bypassing the judicial process.

"Despite claiming public safety is its top priority and public communication is essential to trust, the Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public's demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm," said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau.

The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.

Iowa's newly elected Democratic Senator Josh Turek has called for a full probe into how the lead azide "was allowed to degrade into this critical state and why safer methods of disposal were not pursued".

The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.

On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible. They also said they had been preparing for the event since March.

"Agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the agencies said in a joint statement released on Friday.

Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.

The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".

articles.title: British Asian surgeon Usman Butt wins £101,338 compensation after NHS trust found guilty of race discrimination
articles.summary: Usman Butt, a British Asian surgeon, has been awarded £101,338 in compensation after the NHS trust was found guilty of racial discrimination in hiring practices. This landmark decision highlights systemic issues within the trust regarding treatment of minority ethnic professionals.
articles.body: A British Asian surgeon has been awarded £101,338 in compensation after an employment tribunal found that an NHS trust discriminated against him by overlooking his application for a senior position and appointing a white colleague instead.Usman Butt brought a claim against the Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust after he was denied the role of chair of its surgery division, despite being assessed as suitable for the position. Employment Judge Phil Allen described the recruitment failures as "systemic and numerous".Butt, who joined the trust in August 2015, first applied for the leadership position in May 2022 but was unsuccessful because he lacked the required experience. He was encouraged to apply again in November 2023 when the vacancy reopened, according to Daily Mail.This time, he was the only applicant. He passed the shortlisting stage, met the assessment threshold and was told there was a "99 per cent likelihood" that he would secure the appointment.The surgeon held a master's degree in business administration and a Level 7 senior leadership qualification, both achieved with distinction. He was also recognised as a chartered manager by the Chartered Management Institute.During the selection process, Butt appeared before a nine-member stakeholder panel. The tribunal heard that he delivered a well-structured presentation, answered questions effectively and received the minimum score required from every panel member to be considered appointable.However, some members questioned his experience managing a relatively small department. In February 2024, he received an automated email informing him that he had not been selected. The previous postholder was asked to remain in the position, while a white British doctor was appointed several months later.Butt argued that the successful candidate had less experience and fewer qualifications. He also questioned why she had been asked different interview questions. The trust disputed his allegations of racial discrimination.An independent investigation commissioned by the trust uncovered broader concerns about the treatment of minority ethnic employees.Barrister Carlo Breen, who conducted the inquiry, said he was troubled by accounts from Black, Asian and minority ethnic staff who felt they were treated as "second-class citizens".His report also highlighted concerns about informal networks influencing senior appointments and a lack of confidence in internal systems for raising complaints.Evidence presented to the tribunal included the trust's Workforce Race Equality Standard report, which showed that white candidates were 1.86 times more likely to secure appointments after shortlisting than applicants from minority ethnic backgrounds.A British Asian consultant spinal surgeon, who had previously been unsuccessful in applying for the same leadership position, also told the tribunal that senior roles were frequently allocated through informal networks that excluded minority ethnic doctors.Judge Allen said the trust had failed to provide convincing reasons for rejecting Butt despite his meeting the essential requirements."We found that he had proved primary facts from which we could conclude that the difference in treatment was because of race," the judge said.The tribunal awarded Butt £101,338.74 for financial losses and injury to feelings. He left the Northern Care Alliance in July 2024 after completing his notice period and moved to another NHS trust.Responding to the ruling, Northern Care Alliance Chief Medical Officer Rafik Behair apologised to Butt and said the organisation accepted the tribunal's findings."We are sorry for the discrimination experienced by Mr Butt and fully accept the findings of the Employment Tribunal," Behair said.He acknowledged that the trust needed to address racial inequality and ensure employees received fair opportunities for career progression.The organisation said it would use the judgment to guide its ongoing work on equality and inclusion.You use AI every day. articles.title: China's J-20 study exposes stealth fighters' biggest nightmare: Keeping them combat ready
articles.summary: Developing a fifth-generation stealth fighter takes decades of research, billions of dollars in investment and technological expertise that only a handful
articles.body: Developing a fifth-generation stealth fighter takes decades of research, billions of dollars in investment and technological expertise that only a handful of countries possess.But building one is only half the battle. Keeping these sophisticated machines combat-ready is an equally demanding task for the air forces operating them.China's Chengdu J-20, also known as the 'Mighty Dragon', offers a glimpse into this challenge. A recent study by Chinese researchers has highlighted how damage to radar-absorbing material could weaken a stealth aircraft's ability to evade radar detection.According to a report by Interesting Engineering, the researchers found that losing just 10 per cent of an experimental radar-absorbing coating nearly doubled the amount of microwave energy reflected by the material in laboratory tests.The researchers examined how scratches, surface wear and peeling affect the coating's ability to absorb radar waves. They developed a composite material using carbonyl iron powder and silicone resin, applied it to titanium alloy plates and tested its performance across frequencies ranging from 2 to 18 GHz.The experiments showed that while superficial scratches had a relatively limited impact, deeper wear and coating detachment significantly weakened its radar-absorbing performance.When sections of the coating peeled away, the exposed metal reflected more electromagnetic energy, while the boundaries between damaged and undamaged areas caused additional scattering and diffraction.However, the study did not test the actual stealth coating used on China's J-20. Instead, it demonstrated how damage to a radar-absorbing material can affect its performance, highlighting one of the challenges involved in maintaining low-observable aircraft.Why maintaining a fifth-generation fighter is a difficult taskThe difficulty of maintaining a fifth-generation fighter lies in the fact that its advanced capabilities depend on several interconnected systems that must remain functional at all times.Unlike conventional fighter jets, stealth aircraft require specialised maintenance not only to keep their engines, weapons and avionics operational but also to preserve the low-observable features that make them difficult to detect. A routine repair can sometimes involve additional work to ensure that the aircraft's stealth characteristics are not compromised.The US Air Force's experience with the F-22 Raptor provides a clear example. Its radar-absorbing coating is not simply an external layer of paint but a specialised system of materials that must be carefully applied, inspected and restored.Even routine maintenance involving the removal of an aircraft panel can require additional work because technicians must first remove the coating to access the component and then restore it after the repair.Beyond stealth coatings, maintaining the aircraft's advanced electronics, sensors, engines and software presents another layer of complexity.Fifth-generation fighters rely on integrated systems that allow pilots to combine information from radar, infrared sensors, electronic warfare equipment and other onboard technologies.A problem with a component or software system can restrict the aircraft's ability to perform certain missions, even if it remains capable of flying. Repairs also require specialised diagnostic equipment, technical documentation and trained personnel.The F-35 Lightning II illustrates how these challenges can affect the readiness of an entire fleet. According to a June 2026 report by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO), the F-35 fleet's mission-capable rate declined from 67 per cent in fiscal year 2021 to 44 per cent in fiscal year 2025.Its full mission-capable rate fell from 38 per cent to 25 per cent during the same period. Mission-capable aircraft can perform at least one assigned mission, while full mission-capable aircraft can perform all their assigned missions.The GAO identified shortages of spare parts, delays in component repairs, corrosion and inefficient maintenance practices among the major reasons behind the F-35's persistent readiness problems.The aircraft's continuous technological development has also resulted in multiple configurations, each requiring different maintenance procedures and spare-part requirements. According to US Air Force officials cited in the report, software delays meant some newly accepted F-35s were classified as non-mission capable in fiscal year 2025.The American experience highlights a central challenge of fifth-generation fighter operations: developing an advanced aircraft does not automatically guarantee that it will remain available for combat.Preserving stealth capabilities, maintaining complex electronic systems, securing specialised spare parts and ensuring access to trained technicians require a dedicated support network and sustained investment.For operating air forces, the real test is not simply how many fifth-generation fighters they acquire, but how many they can keep mission-ready when a conflict demands them.

articles.title: US citizen deported to Mexico by Trump administration; DOJ admits mistake in court filing
articles.summary: The Donald Trump administration has admitted in a federal court filing that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after authorities wrongly identified him as
articles.body: The Donald Trump administration has admitted in a federal court filing that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after authorities wrongly identified him as an undocumented immigrant. The admission came nearly seven months after Brian José Morales García, a 25-year-old man from Austin, Texas, was removed from the country where he was born.The US Justice Department acknowledged on Friday that Morales García holds American and Mexican citizenship while simultaneously seeking the dismissal of his lawsuit against the federal government. His legal team has accused immigration authorities of wrongly detaining and deporting him despite his claims that he was born in the US.According to a report by The Guardian, the administration argued that Morales García had travelled to Mexico voluntarily and therefore had no legal grounds to seek damages from the federal government.How US citizen was deported to MexicoMorales García was travelling with his employer to an air-conditioning installation job on April 3 when their vehicle was stopped by state and local law enforcement officers near Fredericksburg, Texas.He was sitting in the passenger seat and did not have identification documents with him. The 25-year-old reportedly told officers that his birth certificate and Social Security card were at his home but they did not accept his explanation and contacted immigration authorities.A US Customs and Border Protection agent, Robert Gil Jr, subsequently checked Mexican records that listed Morales García as having been born in Mexico. The agent also reportedly claimed that Morales García had identified Mexico as his birthplace and noted that he spoke only Spanish, according to court records.He was detained and deported to Mexico on April 7. The Trump administration subsequently described him as an undocumented immigrant in a public statement.DOJ acknowledges dual citizenship while seeking dismissal of lawsuitMorales García's attorneys filed a lawsuit against the federal government on May 1, seeking unspecified damages over his deportation.The lawsuit alleged that immigration agents pressured him into signing paperwork acknowledging that he had entered the US illegally. His lawyers also maintained that his family and friends attempted to provide documents establishing his American citizenship while he was detained, but their efforts were unsuccessful.The Trump administration denied his allegations and maintained that he had travelled to Mexico voluntarily.However, in Friday's court filing, US Attorney for the Western District of Texas Justin Simmons acknowledged that Morales García was allowed to re-enter the US on August 30 after authorities reviewed information about his birthplace."Plaintiff is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico," Simmons wrote in the filing.The judge hearing the case, Robert Lee Pitman, did not immediately rule on the administration's request to dismiss the lawsuit.Report finds US citizens detained during immigration crackdownThe case has emerged amid growing criticism of the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement campaign.A ProPublica investigation published in October 2025 found that immigration agents had detained more than 170 US citizens during the first nine months of Trump's second presidency.The Guardian also reported that cases involving local law enforcement agencies collaborating with federal immigration authorities have raised concerns about officers' understanding of immigration laws.Texas is among the states where local and state agencies participate in the federal government's 287(g) programme, which allows cooperation between local law enforcement and immigration authorities.You use AI every day. articles.title: New Green Card route proposed by Democrats for immigrants facing deportation in US: Who qualifies and what the bill says
articles.summary: A group of Democratic lawmakers has introduced a new immigration bill that could allow certain immigrants facing deportation in the US to obtain Green
articles.body: A group of Democratic lawmakers has introduced a new immigration bill that could allow certain immigrants facing deportation in the US to obtain Green Cards after spending at least 10 years in the country under final removal orders. The proposed legislation, called the Protect Our Neighbors Act, would provide a pathway to lawful permanent residency for eligible immigrants whose deportation orders have remained in place for a decade. It would also introduce an expiration date for certain final removal orders, which currently have no automatic expiry. The bill was introduced on November 19 by California Democratic Representatives Lateefah Simon, Zoe Lofgren, John Garamendi and Juan Vargas. The bill is just a proposal and far from becoming reality.Under the proposal, the attorney general or the homeland security secretary could cancel qualifying removal orders and adjust an immigrant's status to lawful permanent resident. The legislation has been proposed as the Trump administration continues its immigration enforcement campaign, including arrests and deportations of people who have lived in the US for years despite having final removal orders.Who would qualify for the proposed Green Card route?The bill would not offer Green Cards to everyone facing deportation. It would apply only to a specific group of immigrants who meet several conditions. To qualify for the proposed pathway, an immigrant would have to:Have remained in the US for at least 10 years after receiving a final removal, exclusion or deportation order.Have a qualifying removal order based only on certain immigration violations specified under the Immigration and Nationality Act.Have complied with an order of supervision or other conditional release without absconding.Not fall under specified criminal or national security grounds of inadmissibility under federal immigration law.Submit a certified copy of their most recent federal income tax return.The Department of Homeland Security would be allowed to charge a single application fee of no more than $1,200.The bill would also allow the attorney general or homeland security secretary to cancel qualifying removal orders and grant eligible applicants lawful permanent resident status.What happens to deportation orders after 10 years?One of the significant provisions of the Protect Our Neighbors Act is that final removal orders would expire after 10 years.Currently, final deportation orders do not have an automatic expiration date. An immigrant can remain under a final order for years, even if the government does not immediately carry out the deportation.Under the proposed legislation, the Department of Homeland Security could ask an immigration judge to renew an order after the 10-year period. However, the government would have to justify the delay and demonstrate that renewing the order was in the public interest.If a removal order expires and is not renewed, the affected immigrant could petition US Citizenship and Immigration Services for another lawful immigration status for which they are eligible.To use this separate provision, the individual would have to demonstrate at least 10 years of continuous physical presence in the US and meet the bill's criminal eligibility requirements. An expired order could not be renewed while such a petition was pending.The proposal does not mean that every person with a 10-year-old deportation order would automatically receive a Green Card.Why was the bill introduced? Harjit Kaur's deportation to IndiaThe legislation was introduced following cases of long-term immigrants who were deported despite having spent decades building their lives in the US. One case specifically cited by the lawmakers was that of 73-year-old Harjit Kaur, an Indian-origin grandmother who was deported to India in September 2025 after being detained during a routine immigration check-in. Kaur had lived in California for more than 30 years, raising her children and later helping care for her grandchildren. Her deportation became a rallying point for supporters of long-term immigrants facing removal.Representative Lateefah Simon said the proposed legislation would give people such as Kaur, who had worked in her district for decades, an opportunity to move beyond an old removal order and continue building their lives in the US.Kaur's family described her as a pillar of their family and community, saying she had spent more than three decades in America raising her children and grandchildren and had become a grandmother figure to people around her.The proposed legislation, however, would not automatically bring Kaur back to the US. Its Green Card provision requires applicants to meet the physical-presence and other eligibility conditions.How many immigrants have final deportation orders in the US?The proposal could potentially affect a significant number of immigrants. A Congressional Research Service report citing Immigration and Customs Enforcement data estimated that approximately 1.6 million people on ICE's non-detained docket had final orders of removal as of February 26, 2026. A final removal order means an immigration judge or immigration authorities have directed a non-US citizen to leave the country after the relevant administrative appeals have been exhausted or the deadline to appeal has passed.However, having a final removal order does not necessarily mean that deportation will take place immediately. Removal can be delayed or suspended for several reasons, including court proceedings, legal challenges or other administrative circumstances.Will the proposed Green Card bill become law?The Protect Our Neighbors Act faces a difficult legislative path. The legislation was introduced while Republicans still control both chambers of Congress. With the current Congress approaching the end of its term, there are doubts about whether lawmakers will take it up before the end of the year. Democrats are set to take control of both the House and Senate in January 2027 following their midterm election victories. The legislation could therefore return to the congressional agenda next year.Even if Democrats manage to pass the bill, it would still need President Donald Trump's approval. The president has the power to veto legislation. Trump recently told CBS News' 60 Minutes that he would like to work with Democrats on immigration, although he reiterated that his administration would maintain a strong enforcement policy and ruled out an agreement that amounted to amnesty.You use AI every day. articles.title: A UK hotel worker booked a four-week holiday without his manager’s permission, then took his employer to a tribunal over discrimination and unfair dismissal; the judge rejected all his claims
articles.summary: Kitchen porter Dylan Forster, who worked at the Inn on the Lake in Glenridding, booked a four-week trip to South Africa without his manager's approval,
articles.body: Kitchen porter Dylan Forster, who worked at the Inn on the Lake in Glenridding, booked a four-week trip to South Africa without his manager's approval, then took his employer, Lake District Hotels Limited, to an employment tribunal. He claimed disability discrimination and constructive unfair dismissal. The judge dismissed both claims and described his evidence as largely unreliable, citing inconsistencies in his own recollection, in his accounts of events and in the allegations he had raised. The hotel belongs to a small Lake District chain, and Forster knew its busiest periods well from earlier work experience.How the hotel's holiday rules worked and why flights to South Africa were booked before approvalAccording to Personnel Today, Forster began full-time work at the hotel in August 2022 and did not ask for any reasonable adjustments at that point. It later emerged that he was being tested for autism spectrum disorder.His employment contract required holiday dates to be agreed in advance. The hotel's agreement had to be secured at least four weeks beforehand, with approval from the general manager, a head of department or management. The hotel's policy was also to grant only one week's leave during July, August and September, its busiest period, and the tribunal heard that anyone wanting a longer break had to submit a written business case. Every employee received an email setting out these rules in April 2024.Forster lived in hotel accommodation with his partner, Katie Mossop. On 26 June 2024, the couple booked flights for a visit to Kruger National Park with his mother, Julia Forster. They were due to leave on 10 August and return on 12 September.A hand injury, a refused request and a partner's resignation: Events leading up to the disputeShortly before the planned trip, Forster was signed off work with a hand injury. When his manager visited him during that absence, the manager found him playing on his Xbox. Forster claimed the company belittled him and forced him back to work unless he submitted another sick note.He returned in mid-June and, after booking the flights, asked for four weeks' holiday verbally. The hotel refused because it could not spare both Forster and Mossop, who worked as a housekeeper. Mossop resigned on 6 July, although she had managed to secure the time off.WhatsApp messages between Julia Forster and a colleague on maternity leave showed frustration that both employees had not been granted leave. There were also discussions suggesting that his mother's mental illness was the reason for the long holiday, although this was disputed at the tribunal.The resignation notice and the wide-ranging grievances Forster raised against hotel managementOn 6 August, Forster resigned with one week's notice. He told his manager that he would be off sick for seven days due to work-related stress, and that he would be advising human resources of the grievances related to his resignation.Those grievances covered whistleblowing, constructive dismissal and verbal abuse. Forster also accused a manager of antisemitism, age discrimination, injury on duty and disability discrimination. He alleged that management had mocked him, that he had been denied leave on a previous occasion in February 2024, and that he had suffered noise pollution, sleep deprivation, financial abuse and a lack of food.Why the tribunal rejected the discrimination and constructive unfair dismissal claims in fullThe tribunal dismissed the disability discrimination claim because it was brought outside the applicable time limit, although the judge added that it would have failed on its merits anyway.The claim for constructive unfair dismissal, where a worker argues that an employer's conduct left him no real choice but to resign, was also rejected. The tribunal found that the employer had not breached Forster's employment contract, and that it was reasonable for the hotel to refuse his holiday request under its established policy.You use AI every day. articles.title: Burnham does not view Wales as an equal nation, claims first minister
articles.summary: The first minister asks for urgent meeting after Andy Burnham rejected calls for more powers in Cardiff.
articles.body:
The first minister says he wants an urgent meeting with the prime minister after Andy Burnham rejected calls to give more powers to the Welsh government.

Rhun ap Iorwerth said he was "deeply disappointed" and that Burnham "does not view Wales as an equal nation".

Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates urged Burnham to "negotiate around a table" with ap Iorwerth.

In a letter to ap Iorwerth last week, the prime minister said he was "not persuaded" by the case to devolve policing and justice , the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure to Wales.

Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said the UK government believed "devolution must be about more than transferring powers from one government to another".

Trade union body TUC Cymru said it was disappointing calls for further devolution had been "dismissed without any discussion".

In a written statement to Senedd members, the first minister said: "The refusal to even explore the devolution of the crown estate, justice and policing, and rail infrastructure proves that the prime minister does not view Wales as an equal nation.

"The case in favour of Wales having control over these areas of responsibility – just like Scotland – is compelling. Several commissions have argued for the devolution of justice and policing, yet the UK government seemingly prefers to put unionist ideology before hard evidence.

"This government is not interested in more powers for power's sake. The current settlement is unfair, unjust and unsustainable."

In a letter to the prime minister, ap Iorwerth asked the prime minister to reconsider the work of previous reports on the issue.

He said he would "welcome an urgent meeting with you to discuss the evidence and agree a substantive way forward".

Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates called on the Welsh and UK governments to continue talks on the devolution of powers.

He called for "greater detail" on why further devolution of policing was not happening, and said he will be meeting with Burnham himself.

Welsh Labour has not dropped calls for the devolution of justice, the Crown Estate and rail investment.

"You negotiate around a table," he said. "And you don't walk away when work needs to continue. Devolution is a process, not an event and Welsh Labour's position remains clear that we support further devolution to and within Wales."

Skates continued: "Devolution of employment support is vital in getting to grips with the crisis of youth unemployment. The devolution of innovation funding will help strengthen the economy.

"Devolution of youth justice will lead to better integration of youth services and social services and the justice system.

"We need action as fast as possible in bringing these powers to Wales and in ensuring they go to the right people and places.

"On policing, progress is being made, but I want greater detail over why full devolution is not happening as part of the current reforms."

Meanwhile, TUC Cymru's general secretary, Laura Doel, said: "Our focus is on securing the powers and resources needed to improve outcomes for working people. That must include fair funding for Wales.

"These are the long-established views of TUC Cymru and it's disappointing that our calls have been dismissed without any discussion.

"We ask that the UK government does more to respect and engage with the democratic institutions in Wales and listens to the voice of Welsh workers, rather than closing down proposals for further devolution before they have been properly considered."

Kinnock said: "The prime minister's offer reflects our view that devolution must be about more than transferring powers from one government to another and that he instead wants each government to consider, alongside local authority partners, how we can empower Welsh regions to use both reserved and devolved powers to drive economic growth.

articles.title: Israel’s leading contender for prime minister clashes with Netanyahu over Iran strikes
articles.summary: Gadi Eisenkot says Iran poses no immediate threat before a new government forms, as Netanyahu pushes back and Trump weighs renewed strikes on Tehran.
articles.body: The politician tasked by Israel's president to form a new government, Gadi Eisenkot, said Monday that Iran poses no immediate threat requiring military action before a new government is formed, drawing a sharp response from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as President Donald Trump considers renewed strikes against Tehran. The dispute comes amid a political power struggle following last month's Israeli election. Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister, but Eisenkot's allies now control the leadership of the Knesset and key parliamentary committees as negotiations over a new government continue. "Today I see no direct and immediate threat to Israel that requires action before a government is formed," Eisenkot, who previously served as the IDF chief of staff, told his party's Knesset faction, according to an English translation of his Hebrew remarks provided to Fox News Digital. ISRAEL'S POLITICAL SHAKE-UP ENTERS NEW PHASE AS FORMER PM PLAYS KINGMAKER — AND DEADLINE LOOMS He stressed that Iran remains Israel's gravest security threat, particularly its nuclear program. "In my view, the gravest threat from Iran is its stockpile of 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60%," Eisenkot said. "It has yet to be destroyed or removed." He called for the material at a minimum to be placed under strict monitoring. Netanyahu pushed back hours later, accusing political rivals of downplaying the Iranian threat for political reasons. NETANYAHU'S BLOC FALLS SHORT AS LONGTIME ALLIES REPORTEDLY WEIGH MOVE THAT COULD END HIS RULE "The Iranian threats are real," he said before a Likud faction meeting, according to TPS-IL. He renewed his call for a national unity government, signaling room for compromise on ultra-Orthodox military conscription while rejecting a coalition dependent on Arab-led parties. The status of Iran's uranium remains uncertain. The International Atomic Energy Agency last verified approximately 440.9 kilograms enriched to 60% before attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025, but inspectors have since lost continuity of knowledge about the material. The U.S., Britain, France and Germany highlighted that verification gap in a Nov. 19 statement. Adding another perspective Monday, former Mossad director David Barnea urged military action against Iran "as soon as all conditions allow." Speaking at The European Leadership Network Jerusalem conference, Barnea warned that "a diplomatic agreement with the Ayatollah regime will never succeed," according to The Times of Israel, although he also acknowledged the option of giving sanctions more time. TRUMP WARNS OF NEW STRIKES AGAINST IRAN AFTER NEW YEAR, CALLS NEGOTIATORS ‘PROFESSIONAL TAP DANCERS’ The competing assessments followed Trump's comments Sunday to Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst that he was inclined to resume strikes against Iran after the new year if talks failed. Trump called Iranian negotiators "professional tap dancers" and warned that ships challenging the U.S. naval blockade could be sunk. In a response to Fox News Digital, a U.S. official said the administration believes its economic pressure campaign has been effective enough that major military operations are not currently necessary, while emphasizing that Trump retains all options. "As President Trump and Secretary Rubio have stated, our economic pressure campaign is devastating Iran to such an extent that the president does not have any need to conduct major combat operations," the official said on background. "However, President Trump has all options at his disposal to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States." An Israeli source familiar with discussions within the opposition told Fox News Digital that there are assessments that anti-government demonstrations in Iran could intensify as the blockade adds to economic pressure. According to the source, those assessments are contributing to an argument for waiting before launching another major military operation. The forecast has not been independently verified. IRAN VOWS ‘ASTONISHING’ STRIKES AND LIFTS MISSILE-RANGE LIMIT AS US TARGETS LAND ROUTES The blockade has already significantly curtailed Iranian oil exports. Reuters reported Monday that visible Iranian crude exports had dropped to near zero in recent months. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran would use all available means to oppose the restrictions, calling them military aggression, according to Reuters. A new balance of power in the Knesset The disagreement over Iran is unfolding as Eisenkot attempts to turn an electoral advantage into a governing coalition. Israel's Oct. 27 election left no bloc with a governing majority. Eisenkot's four-party alliance won 48 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while Netanyahu's traditional right-wing and religious allies secured 53, including 13 held by the ultra-Orthodox parties. But those alliances have since shifted. United Torah Judaism, which holds seven seats, declined to endorse Netanyahu and has entered coalition negotiations with Eisenkot, leaving the prime minister with just 46 lawmakers formally backing his bid to remain in office. Eisenkot, meanwhile, received the support of 67 lawmakers, including 19 from Arab-led parties, although significant disagreements remain over the composition of a future government. Unlike Congress, Israel has a single-chamber parliament. Although Netanyahu remains in charge of the caretaker government, the new parliamentary majority can advance legislation and exercise oversight without first forming a government. Eisenkot ally Matan Kahana is now Knesset speaker. Former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman heads the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, Liran Avisar Ben Horin chairs the provisional Finance Committee, and Yashar lawmaker Roy Folkman leads the Arrangements Committee, which helps organize parliamentary business. IRAN NUCLEAR DEAL HINGES ON IAEA ACCESS TO LONG-BLOCKED ATOMIC WEAPON SITES, EXPERTS SAY Those appointments have practical consequences. At a Nov. 17 Finance Committee meeting, officials said approximately 1.5 billion shekels in coalition funds remained unallocated. Avisar Ben Horin instructed the Finance Ministry to submit requests involving those funds separately so lawmakers could scrutinize them, according to an official Knesset announcement. The new majority is also advancing legislation to reverse changes to judicial appointments and other measures adopted under Netanyahu, though the bills have not become law. The Israeli source said opposition leaders view control of the committees as an opportunity to restore parliamentary oversight after years in which Netanyahu's coalition dominated the legislative agenda. The source said they also hope to put Eisenkot in a stronger position should Israel return to the polls. Eisenkot said any coalition must respect his core principles, including establishing a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 attacks and expanding mandatory military service. "There will be no compromise on establishing a state commission of inquiry," he said. "There will be no compromise on mandatory service for all." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The debate over when to act against Iran now unfolds alongside another unresolved question in Jerusalem: who will lead Israel when that decision is made. articles.title: SCO: Pakistan set to invite India for culture ministers' meeting
articles.summary: After participating in the SCO inaugural civilisational dialogue in New Delhi, Pakistan is now all set to deliver an invitation to India for a meeting of
articles.body: After participating in the SCO inaugural civilisational dialogue in New Delhi, Pakistan is now all set to deliver an invitation to India for a meeting of the culture ministers it will host under its presidency of the Eurasian bloc early next year. It will be interesting to see how India responds as no Indian minister has visited Pakistan since the Pahalgam terrorist attack.Significantly, Islamabad is also preparing to host the SCO heads of state council summit - where India is usually represented by PM Narendra Modi -next year in late August, after initially considering having it on August 14 – Pakistan's Independence Day. An August 14 summit is unlikely to have seen participation by India at any level.The only significant visit to Pakistan from India after the April 2025 Pahalgam attack was by MEA additional secretary Alok Dimri for a meeting of the SCO national coordinators in September – shortly after Pakistan assumed presidency – to firm up the calendar of events under Islamabad's stewardship.After what is officially called Meeting of Ministers of Culture (SCO-MMC), Pakistan will also host more high-profile meetings of the SCO defence and foreign ministers in the run up to the Islamabad summit in August. The meeting for cultural cooperation among SCO member-states in Pakistan is a relatively low-stakes event for India that keeps political commitments minimal, unlike the foreign and defence high-level gatherings which might raise the political temperature at home.The last minister to visit Pakistan was S Jaishankar for a meeting of the SCO foreign ministers' meeting in October 2024, well before Pahalgam.Amid criticism by the Opposition for hosting Pakistan minister Musadik Malik for the Modi-proposed civilisational dialogue last week, India reiterated there was no dilution of its position on the Indus Waters Treaty that was "put in abeyance" after the Pahalgam attack. India has stressed that SCO cooperation should not be mistaken for bilateral thaw.The visit by Malik passed off smoothly without any bilateral friction as he adhered to the protocol of addressing multilateral SCO themes, rather than raising sensitive bilateral issues.While the key question remains whether Modi will travel to Islamabad for the SCO summit, Indian officials say such a visit is highly improbable at this stage. Any bilateral thaw that might result in Modi's visit requires, as far as India is concerned, a fundamental shift in Pakistan's position on cross-border terrorism. India is seeking tangible progress on its security concerns and doesn't want to create any optics of normalisation when these concerns remain unaddressed.The possibility of a senior minister, most likely Jaishankar, representing India is not ruled out. It would allow India to sustain its active engagement with the SCO, while not being seen as softening its Pakistan policy. Officials point to the fact that there's already a precedent for that. In 2024, it was Jaishankar who attended the heads of summit in Kazakhstan, filling in for the PM.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Ex-Meta engineer who became US citizen and then moved back to Bengaluru after 18 years in America says his children adapted well in India: 'Home is where life takes us'
articles.summary: An Indian-origin former Meta engineer who spent 18 years building a career and family in the US has moved back to Bengaluru with his American-citizen wife
articles.body: An Indian-origin former Meta engineer who spent 18 years building a career and family in the US has moved back to Bengaluru with his American-citizen wife and two children, saying he wanted them to grow up closer to their extended family and Indian culture. Balaji Gururajan, 44, moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to Bengaluru in June with his wife and children, aged 14 and 6. The family rented out their house, sold their cars and furniture before relocating to India, according to a first-person account published by Business Insider on November 19.Gururajan said returning to India had always been in the back of his mind. He originally left Tamil Nadu for the US on an H-1B visa, hoping to work at Microsoft. He initially joined a Sacramento-based nonprofit developing medical software before moving to Microsoft a year later. Then he switched to LinkedIn, where he received his Green Card and later became a US citizen, before joining Meta.He married through a traditional family-arranged match while working at Microsoft. His wife, who has a master's degree in biotechnology, became a homemaker because H-4 spouses were not allowed to work at the time. In 2012, when their son was about five months old, the couple moved to the Bay Area for better professional opportunities and weather and bought a house in Cupertino.Gururajan said raising children in America was different from his own childhood in India, where he grew up surrounded by cousins and relatives. Friends helped fill the gap too some extent but people frequently moved away, leaving the family without the close-knit support system they wanted.The couple decided to move before their son entered ninth grade, fearing a later relocation would disrupt his high school education. Both children were born in the US and had experienced India only through short vacations. Gururajan wanted them to spend time with their grandparents, cousins, aunts and uncles and develop a firsthand connection with Indian culture. His mother had lived with the family in America for nearly five years after he secured her a Green Card, but she felt lonely because she had few people her age to socialise with. His in-laws, meanwhile, were in India and could not relocate to America to live with them.The move came with concerns about leaving California's schools and universities, as well as the children's friends and familiar surroundings. The family kept their Cupertino home as a backup.Gururajan said life in Bengaluru has been more comfortable than he expected. The family pays around $1,050 in monthly rent for a home in a gated community and another $260 for daily household help. Unlike their life in America, where both parents handled domestic responsibilities themselves, he now has more time to take his daughter to the park and help his son with schoolwork. Speaking about the adjustment to life in India, he said the children have also adjusted better than expected. His son likes his new school and has made friends, while his daughter, who initially cried about starting at another school, has become comfortable. Both attend an English-speaking school following an international curriculum.Traffic and infrastructure problems are there, he acknowldged but India changed significantly, he said. After working almost continuously for 20 years, he is now taking a sabbatical and considering whether to return to similar professional roles or start something of his own.Gururanjan said they are also open about their children going back to the US later because home is where life takes everyone.You use AI every day.
