articles.title: A 16-metre bamboo hedge sparked an Australian neighbours' fight over a damaged fence, blocked gutters and lost sunlight; on November 19, a court ordered removal within one metre and split fence costs equally
articles.summary: A common backyard privacy hedge has become the unlikely centerpiece of a legal battle in Australia, turning a neighborhood boundary into a dispute about
articles.body: A common backyard privacy hedge has become the unlikely centerpiece of a legal battle in Australia, turning a neighborhood boundary into a dispute about towering bamboo, damaged fencing, clogged gutters and complaints about lost sunlight. The case of applicant Leonard Clyde Lloyd and neighbor Susan Boyd Valstar, which eventually came before the Land and Environment Court of New South Wales, was one of growing concern about increasing vegetation on the neighbour’s property. In a ruling on November 19, 2026, the court dealt with the competing property concerns, ordering the removal of bamboo within one meter and directing the neighbors to share the cost of replacing their dividing fence.Property dispute over bamboo hedgeIn Lloyd v Valstar [2026] NSWLEC 1764 the bamboo was growing on the boundary line between the parties’ properties. The hedge was said to be about 16 meters high, raising concerns about its effect on neighboring property.The applicant complained of damage to property from the bamboo, leaves falling into the gutters and the deterioration of the dividing fence, the Land and Environment Court of New South Wales heard. There was also concern that the height and location of the vegetation would reduce the amount of sunlight entering the adjoining dwelling.The dispute required the court to assess the extent of the damage and to determine which issues required legal intervention rather than routine property maintenance.Inspected for blocked gutters and fence damageThe court considered whether fallen bamboo leaves blocking gutters constituted actionable property damage under the Trees (Disputes Between Neighbors) Act 2006.But the Land and Environment Court of New South Wales said problems that could be avoided by reasonable maintenance, including regular cleaning of gutters, would not normally warrant intervention under the legislation. Even the presence of overhanging vegetation was not enough to establish damage.The dividing fence was a different matter. Although bamboo contributed to some of the degradation, the court found that the bamboo’s general condition was largely a result of its age and exposure to the elements. Vegetation was only a minor contributor to the fence damage.The court therefore considered it appropriate to share the cost of replacement between the two owners of the properties rather than make one neighbor solely liable.Sunlight complaint fails to meet legal standardsAnother major concern for the court was the effect of the bamboo hedge on natural light. The applicant claimed relief under the law for serious tree obstruction of sunlight to his house.However, when considering the complaint, the Land and Environment Court of New South Wales, made a distinction between direct sunlight and general ambient daylight.The court noted that the bamboo hedge was located to the south of the south-facing windows of the applicant. Due to this position, it could not be determined that the vegetation created a significant obstruction to the direct sunlight that would reach these windows.The court accordingly refused to make the orders sought on the basis of obstruction of sunlight. The decision emphasized the need to show that there was actual interference with the direct sunlight and not just a reduction in daylight.Court orders bamboo removal, equal fence paymentsThe court did not find all the grievances of the applicant acceptable but enough reasons to order targeted intervention in respect of the bamboo. The ruling ordered the removal of the relevant bamboo within one meter of the property boundary.In relation to the dispute over fencing, the Land and Environment Court of New South Wales ordered the dividing fence be replaced, and both neighbors contribute equally toward the costs.The decision took into account the relatively minor contribution of bamboo to the deterioration of the fence and the effects of aging and weathering.The ruling on 19 November in Lloyd v Valstar demonstrates that there can be a number of separate legal issues arising in Australian disputes over neighborhood vegetation, including property damage, maintenance obligations, fencing obligations and sunlight access.According to the circumstances and evidence, the Land and Environment Court of New South Wales allowed limited bamboo removal, dismissed the sunlight application, and ordered equal fencing costs.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. articles.title: NIA court frees 4 held for 2020 Srinagar terror attack that killed 2 soldiers
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: The killing of two Army soldiers in a Nov 2020 terrorist attack on the outskirts of Srinagar was established, but the prosecution failed to
articles.body: SRINAGAR: The killing of two Army soldiers in a Nov 2020 terrorist attack on the outskirts of Srinagar was established, but the prosecution failed to prove that the four arrested men had helped the terrorists, a special NIA court said Monday while acquitting them under UAPA.Special NIA judge Manjeet Rai acquitted Nasir Ahmad Dar, Zahid Ahmad Allai, Usman Ahmad Sheikh and Humayun Ahmad Sheikh of charges under sections 13, 18, 19 and 39 of UAPA. He ordered their release forthwith if they were not required in any other case.The court said there was no evidence that the accused conspired with, sheltered or supported the terrorists, communicated with them or were present near the attack site. No arms, explosives or other material were found in their possession, making the statutory presumption under section 43E of UAPA inapplicable.The prosecution case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence, with no eyewitness linking the four men to the attack. Citing Supreme Court’s 1984 judgement in Sharad Birdhichand Sarda vs State of Maharashtra, NIA court reiterated that every circumstance in a case based on circumstantial evidence must be fully established and the chain must point exclusively to the accused’s guilt.The court said prosecution had established that the attack killed two soldiers and a service rifle was lost, but the gravity of the crime could not substitute for legal proof.“The loss of lives is a grave one and the anxiety of the prosecuting agency to bring every person responsible to book is understandable. But the law requires that guilt be proved by legal evidence and the gravity of the crime only heightens the need for such proof,” it said.The four men are residents of Zainakote, where the attacked happened near the HMT factory on Nov 26, 2020, when terrorists fired at an Army road opening party, killing constable Rattan Singh and sepoy Des Raj. The attackers took away a service rifle.Police registered an FIR, naming seven accused. The four men were arrested after questioning several alleged “overground” operatives of terrorist groups. They remained in judicial custody throughout the trial and appeared before the court through video conferencing.The other three, identified as Abrar Nadeem alias Khitaab, Muslim alias Hanzala alias Babar and Asrar alias Mahmood alias Abdullah, were described as Pakistani terrorists in the chargesheet. They were killed in separate shootouts in Sopore of Baramulla district and Malura outside Srinagar in June 2021, and proceedings against them were abated. The snatched rifle was later found in a separate case in Sopore.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Children are not toys, hear their voice in custody battles, says SC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Observing children should not be treated as toys in the custody battle between parents, Supreme Court Monday said such cases should not be
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Observing children should not be treated as toys in the custody battle between parents, Supreme Court Monday said such cases should not be decided only on a legalistic basis but children's choice should be given due weightage while deciding the case.A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh set aside orders passed by a family court and Madras HC for granting custody of two minor boys, aged 16 and 14 years, under Guardians and Wards Act. The court passed the order after having an interaction with the boys who expressed their preference to remain with their mother. The court granted visitation right to the father."The object and purpose of the Act is not merely physical custody of the minor, but due protection of the right of the ward's health, maintenance and education. When the court is confronted with conflicting demands made by the parents, it has not only to look at the issue on a legalistic basis. In such matters human factors are also relevant. It is often said that children are not mere chattels, nor are they toys for their parents," the bench said."In the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the considered opinion that the children should not be separated from their mother with whom they have developed a strong natural bond over the years keeping into account the predominant criterion of paramount consideration of the welfare of the child," it said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: MS NOW host threatens to eject ‘tech bro’ guest during Jensen Huang debate, warns 'The door's right there!'
articles.summary: Stephanie Ruhle demanded respect during a heated MS NOW panel as Jason Calacanis defended Nvidia’s reinstated CEO against Yale lecturer Gautam Mukunda.
articles.body: MS NOW host Stephanie Ruhle rebuked several guests on Monday's episode of "Money, Power, Politics" for questioning each other’s credibility and demanded they leave if they refused to follow her rules. Nvidia’s board unanimously reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO after input from senior U.S. government officials indicated his return poses no national security risk following an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. President Donald Trump praised Nvidia's decision on Truth Social, calling Huang a "great patriot and a national treasure" while urging the chipmaker to complete its internal export-control investigation. But the guests on Ruhle’s show were more divided. American internet entrepreneur and angel investor Jason Calacanis defended the reinstated CEO, arguing that someone as wealthy and successful as Huang would never risk committing treason. TRUMP ‘DIRECTLY AND INDIRECTLY’ INTERVENED TO GET NVIDIA’S CEO REINSTATED, POTUS SAYS In response, Yale School of Management lecturer and Bloomberg Opinion columnist Gautam Mukunda argued that there were credible accusations that Huang may have engaged in a criminal conspiracy to violate export control laws. He also dismissed the idea that the world’s third-richest person would not engage in such conduct as "absurd." Calacanis interjected, dismissing the argument as "how Yale elites think." Ruhle immediately cut in to scold him, saying she would not allow guests to label one another. "Hold on," she told Calacanis. "What we're not going to do here is say that because he works at Yale, he's some sort of elite. What we are not going do is label anyone. Just like I'm not gonna label you a ‘tech bro.’" "I'm going to say ‘Jason's an investor who's here, and you're welcome to be here and share your opinions.’ But you're not gonna sit at my table and say ‘you're a Yale elite so you think this,'" she scolded before warning, "If that's what you're going to do, then the door's right there!" TRUMP DEFENDS JENSEN HUANG'S CREDIBILITY, NVIDIA'S FUTURE AFTER BOARD REINSTATED CEO, SAYS 'SEX SELLS' MS NOW business analyst Ron Insana then went after Calacanis’ credibility, saying he was "so tired of this Silicon Valley BS." As the panel laughed, Ruhle scolded her guests again and urged them to show each other respect. "Give your opinion based on the facts that you know," she told Insana. articles.title: US blacklists Nvidia-linked Megaspeed over alleged AI chip diversion to China
articles.summary: The US commerce department on Monday added Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International and six other firms from Singapore, Malaysia
articles.body: The US commerce department on Monday added Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International and six other firms from Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand to its trade blacklist over alleged diversion of artificial intelligence (AI) chips to China, intensifying scrutiny of the Nvidia controversy.Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner, has been under investigation by US authorities since 2024 over allegations that it diverted AI chips to China.Its addition to the Entity List means the companies will require approval from the US commerce department to obtain American exports, with such requests likely to be denied, Reuters reported.The move followed criticism from lawmakers and administration officials over the delay in blacklisting Megaspeed."The department of commerce still needs to explain ⁠to Commerce why this took so long," Senator Pete Ricketts, a Nebraska Republican, said in a post on X. A Commerce Department official said the six other companies added to the list also had links to Megaspeed.Megaspeed came under the spotlight earlier this month after reports emerged about an alleged affair between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, a former senior executive at the Singapore-based company.US authorities suspect Alice Huang of being a Chinese spy, although China has dismissed the allegations as "groundless".Following the reports, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent criticised the Commerce Department for not placing Megaspeed on the Entity List earlier and questioned whether Nvidia had adequately monitored its customers and chip sales.Nvidia has said it recently formed an export control committee to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. In a statement last week, the company said it conducts legitimate and lawful business and complies with US export controls.It also said Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed in August 2025.The US justice department and commerce department last week issued a joint statement saying they would "bring ​the full extent of ⁠the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred."Democratic lawmakers have also opened a probe into the influence Nvidia may have exerted over the Commerce Department's investigation into Megaspeed.The blacklisting comes as Huang has returned as Nvidia's CEO after stepping down two weeks ago amid reports about his alleged relationships, including an extramarital affair with Alice Huang. The latest action comes amid broader US efforts to restrict China's access to advanced AI chips and technology.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Massachusetts homeowner installed 13 surveillance cameras and four speed bumps on a shared driveway; a court ordered their removal after neighbours said they felt intimidated and their Corvette could not cross the bumps
articles.summary: A Westfield homeowner who installed surveillance cameras and speed bumps along a driveway used by his neighbours has been ordered to remove them.
articles.body: A Westfield homeowner who installed surveillance cameras and speed bumps along a driveway used by his neighbours has been ordered to remove them. Richard Tersavich owns the land beneath the driveway, but Michael and Sharon Greany hold a legal right to use it. A Land Court judge found that the cameras and speed bumps interfered with that right, and the Appeals Court left the order in place on 29 June 2026. His separate claim for reimbursement for repair work on a water pipe under the driveway failed, and the judgment went against him on every claim.How Massachusetts homeowner’s surveillance cameras and speed bumps spark neighbour disputeAccording to the Appeals Court of Massachusetts decision published by FindLaw, Tersavich and his wife, Joanne, bought their property off Eastwood Drive in May 2018. The Greanys bought the adjoining property the following month and moved in with their two children, aged six and ten at the time of the trial. Every journey to either home runs along a driveway that sits entirely on Tersavich's land. It rises for more than 200 feet from Eastwood Drive, then levels out and continues at least another 200 feet past his house to the Greany property.The deeds to both properties give the Greanys an easement over the driveway, meaning a legal right to cross a neighbour's land, for access to and from Eastwood Drive by vehicle or otherwise. A Shared Maintenance Agreement recorded in 1990 also requires both households to share the cost of reasonable and necessary repairs to the driveway and the utilities they have in common.Why the cameras went up in 2020, how many pointed at the driveway and how the Greanys respondedIn 2020, after a disagreement that led to the police being called, Tersavich installed surveillance cameras along the driveway. The judge found that at one point 13 cameras were installed on his property, with at least four pointed directly at the driveway. The Greanys told the court that the monitoring made them so uncomfortable that they limited their use of the driveway and asked for one child's bus stop to be changed so the child would not be recorded.Tersavich told the court that the cameras were there to provide security for his family. The trial judge did not accept that account and found that the cameras, together with signs posted along the driveway, were installed solely to intimidate the Greanys in the hope that they would use the driveway less often. The judge described the cameras as an unjustified invasion of the family's privacy, a phrase the Appeals Court later said was a characterisation of his conduct rather than a separate privacy claim.Four speed bumps, a Corvette that could not cross them and what the owner told the courtIn spring 2021, Tersavich installed four speed bumps, roughly fifty feet apart, along the flat stretch of the driveway. Joanne Tersavich told the court that they were a safety measure to slow the cars and delivery trucks heading to the Greany property, although she offered no evidence of how fast vehicles travelled. Tersavich himself told the court that the bumps were meant partly to slow traffic and partly to minimise the number of cars using the driveway.The trial judge concluded that the bumps were installed to deter the Greanys and their visitors from using the driveway. The judge also noted evidence that the Greanys could not drive their Corvette over them because of their height and because spikes sometimes protruded from the bumps, raising concern about damage to the vehicle. The judge did not impose a blanket ban, though: the parties remain free to agree on speed bumps of a particular type, size and number.How the Land Court trial unfolded and why the Appeals Court rejected each of Tersavich's argumentsThe Greanys filed their case in the Land Court in May 2022 and asked for the cameras and speed bumps to be removed. The judge viewed the properties and driveway on 16 May 2024, and the trial began four days later. The resulting order covered all cameras located along the driveway or pointing towards the Greanys' property, along with the speed bumps on the driveway.On appeal, Tersavich argued that the Greanys had not proved a standalone invasion of privacy claim. The Appeals Court disagreed, saying the judge's wording simply framed his conduct, installing cameras to intimidate, as a material interference with the right to use the driveway. It also rejected his argument that the interference was slight because the Greanys kept using the driveway, albeit less. The judge had found that the cameras got in the way of using it without constant surveillance or the unease of not knowing where the recordings were stored.The court found the removal order was not overbroad, because it did not require the removal of cameras directed solely at Tersavich's property, such as one facing his front door or backyard. His reimbursement argument offered no legal reasoning or case law, and the invoice he submitted did not show any amount paid or whether the repairs were reasonable and necessary.You use AI every day. articles.title: 100 intelligence reports, $150,000 payoff: China sentences official to death for spying
articles.summary: China has sentenced a government official to death for allegedly leaking state secrets to a foreign country after he was recruited by a foreign
articles.body: China has sentenced a government official to death for allegedly leaking state secrets to a foreign country after he was recruited by a foreign intelligence agency while serving overseas, according to a report published on Monday by a state-affiliated social media account.The official, identified only by his surname Ma, allegedly sent more than 100 intelligence reports to his foreign handler after returning to China. Of these, 35 were later classified as state secrets. He received more than one million yuan ($150,000) for his activities, which the report described as a "long-running" operation, Reuters reported.The report was published by Baomiguan, an account overseen by China's National Administration of State Secrets Protection. It said an unspecified court had sentenced Ma to death and ordered the confiscation of all his personal property.However, the report did not identify the organisation for which Ma worked or the foreign intelligence agency involved. It also did not disclose when he was arrested or sentenced, how long he had been spying, or whether the execution had been carried out. Reuters said it could not independently verify the report.The case was widely circulated by Chinese state media and briefly became the top-trending topic on the social media platform Weibo on Monday morning.China's state secrecy regulator and Ministry of State Security (MSS), the country's main intelligence and counter-espionage agency, have increasingly used social media to warn officials against becoming informants or spies for foreign governments. The MSS also regularly publishes anonymised accounts of officials accused of espionage.The reports typically describe cases involving officials who are allegedly recruited through personal relationships, financial incentives or coercion. While many result in prison sentences, some carry the death penalty.Monday's post said the "struggle on the hidden front has never ceased, and intelligence agencies' methods have become increasingly deceptive", Reuters reported.It urged officials to remain alert to national security risks, strengthen party discipline and confidentiality awareness, follow workplace rules and guard against being targeted or exploited.The report comes after the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) released videos in 2025 and 2026 seeking informants within China's bureaucracy and military. The videos included instructions in Chinese on how to establish secure contact with the agency. Beijing described them as a "damning confession" of the CIA's efforts to obtain other countries' secrets.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: What Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO means for Colette Kress, here's what company says
articles.summary: Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as the chief executive officer, bringing an end to a turbulent period which witnessed chief Colette Kress lead the
articles.body: Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as the chief executive officer, bringing an end to a turbulent period which witnessed chief Colette Kress lead the AI chipmaker as interim CEO for 11 days. According to a CNBC report, along with Huang’s return, Nvidia also confirmed that Kress will continue in her role as chief financial officer, signalling the board’s continued confidence in one of the company’s longest-serving senior executives. The return of Jensen Huang came after he stepped down earlier this month following revelations related to extramarital relationships. The announcement sparked a strong market reaction, with Nvidia shares surging 31% on Monday while the Nasdaq gained more than 6%, reflecting investor enthusiasm for the comeback of the company’s co-founder and long-time leader.How the week unfoldedThe board accepted Huang’s resignation on November 11 and appointed Kress, 59, as interim CEO. Huang, 63, resigned following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares jumped 31% on Monday and the Nasdaq rose more than 6% after the announcement, and employees cheered Huang as he returned to the office.Kress joined Nvidia as finance chief in September 2013, after stints at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments. She holds about 4.775 million shares, worth roughly $778 million at Monday’s close. As CFO she oversees the balance sheet of a company that is financing many of the infrastructure deals behind the AI buildout, arrangements that have raised concerns about circular financing and exposure to a slowdown.Colette Kress to reamin CFO after a brief stint as interim CEOWhile Huang has returned as CEO, president and board director with immediate effect, Nvidia said Kress will remain CFO. The 59-year-old executive, who joined Nvidia in September 2013 after leadership roles at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments, took charge of the company during one of the most challenging periods in its history.Kress currently holds approximately 4.775 million Nvidia shares directly and indirectly, giving her a stake valued at about $778 million based on Monday’s closing price. Her interim leadership role put her at the centre of Nvidia’s efforts to reassure investors, employees and customers amid uncertainty surrounding Huang’s departure.Kress sought to reassure investorsDuring Nvidia’s first earnings call following Huang’s resignation, Kress attempted to calm market concerns by raising the company’s fiscal 2028 revenue growth forecast to roughly 75%, up from an earlier estimate of 70%.She repeatedly stressed that operations remained on track and characterised the situation as “business as usual.” In media appearances, Kress said customer demand for Nvidia’s AI products continued to rise and that major clients remained committed to the company despite the leadership upheaval. At an all-hands employee meeting after Huang’s exit, she struck an optimistic tone, encouraging staff to focus on the future and highlighting upcoming pay increases.Some insiders defend KressNot everyone shared the criticism. According to CNBC, one former Nvidia employee praised Kress for handling the crisis with “skill and grace” and helping reassure both employees and industry partners during a period of uncertainty.The person also expressed confidence that Kress would remain a key member of Nvidia’s leadership team after Huang’s return, describing her as a “fantastic CFO” who retains Huang’s trust.What Nvidia and Huang saidIn the official announcement confirming his reinstatement, Huang publicly thanked Kress for leading the company during his absence. “I am grateful for Colette leading NVIDIA during this period,” Huang said. The statement appears to settle speculation over Kress’ future at the company, with Nvidia formally confirming that she will continue as CFO while Huang resumes control of the AI chip giant.For investors, the board’s decision restores the executive who has led Nvidia through its transformation into one of the world’s most valuable companies. For Kress, it means a return to overseeing the finances of the company she helped guide through a brief but highly scrutinised leadership crisis.The investigation into Jensen Huang will still run its courseHuang's return does not end the probe. A committee made up only of independent directors, working with independent counsel, is looking into the foreign intelligence reports. The board said the investigation will proceed to its conclusion. Huang has said he fully supports it and will cooperate.Nvidia is also adding new layers of oversight. The board recently set up a National Security and Export Control Committee, again made up only of independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. It is bringing in counsel with national security experience, who will hire specialist advisers of their own. The company has also started a search for a new Chief Compliance Officer, who will report to the board's Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee.Nvidia said it will keep cooperating with ongoing government investigations. Huang and general counsel Tim Teter are scheduled to answer questions from US House committees behind closed doors on December 1 and 2.Fearless legend or grounded realist?
